title: Vectors and Slices
intro: `Vec<T>` is a list that can grow. `&[T]`, called a slice, is a borrowed window into part of one.

coming_from.go: `Vec<T>` is a slice that you own: `v.push(x)` replaces `v = append(v, x)` and changes the `Vec` in place. `&w[1..3]` is the same no-copy window as `w[1:3]`, but it is read-only unless you ask for `&mut`, it has no capacity to append into, and the compiler refuses to `push` to `w` while the window is in use. That rules out the `append` aliasing surprise.
coming_from.kotlin: `Vec<T>` is your `MutableList`, and `&w[1..3]` is a view like `subList(1, 3)`. While the view is in use, the compiler refuses to add to `w`, where on the JVM `subList` can throw `ConcurrentModificationException` later. A `Vec` without `mut` is a list you cannot push to or assign into, which a Kotlin `List` does not promise.
coming_from.python: `Vec<T>` is your `list`, but every item has the same type and there are no negative indexes. `&w[1..3]` is a borrowed view, not a copy like Python's slicing, and an index past the end panics (Python raises `IndexError`).
coming_from.typescript: `Vec<T>` is your `T[]` and `push` adds to the end the same way. `&w[1..3]` is a borrowed view rather than a copy like `slice`, and an index past the end panics instead of giving `undefined`.
coming_from.java: `Vec<i32>` is an `ArrayList<Integer>` whose items are plain numbers stored side by side (Java's `List<int>` does not compile). `&w[1..3]` is like `subList(1, 3)`, but Rust refuses to compile code that changes the `Vec` while a slice of it is in use, where Java can throw `ConcurrentModificationException` at run time.
coming_from.csharp: `Vec<T>` is `List<T>`, and `&w[1..3]` is a borrowed view like a `Span<T>`, not a copy like `GetRange`. While that view is alive, Rust won't let you `push` to the list.
coming_from.c: `Vec<T>` is your pointer, length and capacity struct with `push` and `realloc` built in, and `&[T]` is a pointer plus a length. The compiler won't let you keep a pointer into a `Vec` across a `push` that might move it, and `v[i]` is bounds-checked.
coming_from.cpp: `Vec<T>` is `std::vector<T>`, and `&[T]` is `std::span<const T>`. The difference is that holding a reference or span into a vector, calling `push` and then using the reference is a compile error, not undefined behaviour. `v[i]` checks its bounds where `std::vector`'s `operator[]` does not by default.

notes: `{:?}` prints a whole Vec. Normal `{}` printing is not defined for lists.
`v[10]` on a short Vec crashes the program with a panic. `v.get(10)` returns an Option instead.
A Vec is three numbers on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) plus the items on the heap. A slice `&[T]` is two numbers: a pointer and a length.
`let x = v[0];` copies a number out of a `Vec<i32>`, but for a `Vec<String>` it is a compile error: borrow with `&v[0]` or copy with `v[0].clone()`.
`v.sort()` needs items that can always be ranked, and `f64` cannot (`NaN`). For floats, write `v.sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b))`.

gotcha.title: Taking a String out of a list by index
gotcha.looks_fine: In most languages `names[0]` hands you the item, and the list keeps it too.
gotcha.rust_sees: `names[0]` is a slot inside the list's buffer, and the list owns the `String` that lives there. `let first = names[0]` would move the `String` out and leave a hole in the list. The list would still free every slot when it is dropped, so that `String` would be freed twice.
gotcha.why: Nothing is wrong with wanting the first name. The other languages quietly choose for you: share a reference, copy a pointer, or copy the whole text. Rust asks which one you mean. `&names[0]` borrows it, `names[0].clone()` makes a second copy, `names.remove(0)` takes it out of the list, and `std::mem::take(&mut names[0])` takes it and leaves an empty `String` behind. A `Vec<i32>` has no such error, because an `i32` is copied, not moved. Any item that is not `Copy` behaves like the `String`, a struct or a row of a `Vec<Vec<T>>` included.

go.says: Go prints `ana of 2`. A Go string is a small header (pointer and length) and its bytes never change, so `first := names[0]` copies the header and both names share the text safely.

kotlin.says: Kotlin prints `ana of 2`. `first` and the list slot refer to the same `String` object. Strings can't be changed, so sharing is harmless, and the garbage collector keeps the object alive while either refers to it.

python.says: Python prints `ana of 2`. `first` and the list slot are two names for the same string object, which can't be changed, so sharing is harmless.

typescript.says: Prints `ana of 2`. `first` is a string value. Strings never change in place, so it makes no visible difference whether the engine copies or shares the characters.

java.says: Java prints `ana of 2`. `first` and the list slot refer to the same `String` object. A `String` can't be changed, and the garbage collector keeps it alive while either refers to it.

csharp.says: C# prints `ana of 2`. `first` and the list slot refer to the same `string` object, which can't be changed, and the garbage collector keeps it alive.

c.says: C prints `ana of 2`. `first` copies the pointer, so both point at the same text. Here the text is a string literal. With heap text, nothing in the code says which of the two pointers must `free` it, and freeing it through one leaves the other dangling.

cpp.says: C++ prints `ana of 2`. `std::string first = names[0]` copies the whole string, so the two are independent. To take it without copying you write `std::move(names[0])`, which leaves `names[0]` valid but unspecified.

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var v []int
	v = append(v, 10)
	v = append(v, 20)

	w := []int{1, 2, 3}
	w = append(w, 4)

	part := w[1:3] // a window onto w's array, no copy

}

check-go.go.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
	"sort"
)

func must(ok bool, what string) {
	if !ok {
		panic(what)
	}
}

func main() {
	v := []int{3, 1, 2}
	v = append(v, 4)
	w := []int{7, 8}
	v = append(v, w...)
	must(slices.Equal(v, []int{3, 1, 2, 4, 7, 8}), "append")
	must(len(v) == 6 && cap(v) >= 6, "len cap")

	z := make([]int, 3)
	must(slices.Equal(z, []int{0, 0, 0}), "make n")
	must(len(make([]int, 0, 10)) == 0 && cap(make([]int, 0, 10)) == 10, "make cap")

	must(v[len(v)-1] == 8, "last")
	v = v[:len(v)-1]
	must(len(v) == 5, "pop")

	v = append(v[:1], v[2:]...)
	must(slices.Equal(v, []int{3, 2, 4, 7}), "remove")
	v = slices.Insert(v, 1, 5)
	must(slices.Equal(v, []int{3, 5, 2, 4, 7}), "insert")

	s := slices.Clone(v)
	slices.Sort(s)
	must(slices.Equal(s, []int{2, 3, 4, 5, 7}), "sort")
	pos, found := slices.BinarySearch(s, 4)
	must(pos == 2 && found, "binary search")
	pos, found = slices.BinarySearch(s, 6)
	must(pos == 4 && !found, "binary search miss")
	must(slices.Contains(s, 5) && slices.Index(s, 5) == 3 && slices.Index(s, 99) == -1, "contains index")

	names := []string{"kiwi", "fig", "banana"}
	sort.Slice(names, func(i, j int) bool { return len(names[i]) < len(names[j]) })
	must(slices.Equal(names, []string{"fig", "kiwi", "banana"}), "sort.Slice")

	slices.Reverse(s)
	must(slices.Equal(s, []int{7, 5, 4, 3, 2}), "reverse")
	runs := slices.Compact([]int{1, 1, 2, 2, 1})
	must(slices.Equal(runs, []int{1, 2, 1}), "compact")

	window := s[1:3]
	window[0] = 99
	must(s[1] == 99, "a subslice shares the array")
	dst := make([]int, 2)
	must(copy(dst, []int{1, 2, 3}) == 2 && slices.Equal(dst, []int{1, 2}), "copy copies the shorter length")
	cl := slices.Clone(dst)
	cl[0] = 9
	must(dst[0] == 1, "Clone is independent")
	dst = dst[:0]
	must(len(dst) == 0, "s[:0] empties")
	arr := [3]int{1, 2, 3}
	arr2 := arr
	arr2[0] = 9
	must(arr[0] == 1, "arrays copy on assignment")
	fmt.Println("all checks passed")
}

check-kt.kt.code:
fun must(ok: Boolean, what: String) {
    if (!ok) throw AssertionError(what)
}

fun main() {
    val v = mutableListOf(3, 1, 2)
    v.add(4)
    must(v.removeLastOrNull() == 4, "removeLastOrNull")
    must(mutableListOf<Int>().removeLastOrNull() == null, "removeLastOrNull on empty")
    must(v.removeAt(1) == 1 && v == listOf(3, 2), "removeAt")
    v.add(1, 5)
    must(v == listOf(3, 5, 2) && v.last() == 2 && v.lastOrNull() == 2, "add last")
    must(v.getOrNull(99) == null && v.size == 3 && 5 in v, "getOrNull size in")
    v.addAll(listOf(7, 8))
    v.removeAll { it == 7 }
    must(v == listOf(3, 5, 2, 8), "removeAll")
    must(v.subList(1, 3) == listOf(5, 2), "subList")
    v.sort()
    must(v == listOf(2, 3, 5, 8), "sort")
    v.sortBy { -it }
    must(v == listOf(8, 5, 3, 2), "sortBy")
    val words = mutableListOf("kiwi", "fig", "banana")
    words.sortWith(compareBy { it.length })
    must(words == listOf("fig", "kiwi", "banana"), "sortWith")
    val ro: List<Int> = v
    must(ro.toMutableList() == v && ro.sorted() == listOf(2, 3, 5, 8), "toMutableList sorted")
    val sub = v.subList(1, 3)
    v[1] = 42
    must(sub[0] == 42, "subList is a view")
    println("all checks passed")
}
